## Demographic data

HPVsim includes pre-downloaded demographic data, including:

 * Population sizes from 1950-2100 from the UN's World Population Projections;
 * Birth rates from 1950-2100 from the World Bank;
 * Age- and sex-specific mortality rates from 1950-2100 from the UN's World Population Projections.

As we saw in Tutorial 1, you load these data simply by using the `location` parameter. HPVsim ships demographic data (age structure, births, deaths) for any country in the UN World Population Prospects; just pass the country name (case-insensitive). Network calibration is location-agnostic by default — analysis scripts supply their own per-country network parameters.

When a `location` is set, HPVsim uses these data to seed the initial age/sex pyramid and to drive births, deaths, and age-specific migration over the course of the run. The migration module pins the simulated age pyramid to the target population trajectory each year; the resulting immigrant/emigrant flows are reported under `sim.results.agemigration`.

## People and contact network layers

Agents in HPVsim are contained in an object called `People`, which holds all of the agents' properties (age, sex, disease state, ...), together with the machinery for moving them from one state to another (e.g., from susceptible to infected).

HPV transmits via sexual contact, represented in HPVsim by a sexual network that lets agents interact. For the moment, HPVsim only models heterosexual partnerships. The default sexual network (`hpv.SexualNetwork`) has three contact layers — marital, casual, and one-off — each with its own properties characterizing sexual contact (partnership duration, age-mixing preferences, concurrency, and so on). The network is created automatically from the `location`'s network parameters when you build a `hpv.Sim`.

## A worked example

Below we build and run a sim, then inspect the population and network it produced. Because demographics evolve over the run, the number of alive agents changes over time:

```{python}
#| collapsed: false
import numpy as np
import hpvsim as hpv

hpv.options(jupyter=True, verbose=False)

sim = hpv.Sim(
    n_agents=20_000,
    start=1970,
    stop=2020,
    location='nigeria',
    rand_seed=1,
)
sim.run()

# Population size over time (driven by births, deaths, and migration)
print('Alive at start:', int(sim.results.n_alive[0]))
print('Alive at end:  ', int(sim.results.n_alive[-1]))

sim.plot();
```

To assess the effect of stochasticity, it is often useful to run several sims with different random seeds and combine them. Starsim's `MultiSim` does this — pass an `hpv.Sim` and a number of runs, then reduce with `mean()` (or `median()`):

```{python}
import starsim as ss

msim = ss.MultiSim(hpv.Sim(n_agents=10_000, start=1970, stop=2020,
                           location='nigeria'), n_runs=3)
msim.run(parallel=False, verbose=False)
msim.mean()
msim.plot();
```
